title: Transfer: Maximum Product Subarray
oneLiner: The largest product of a contiguous run. Kadane's one pass still works, but a negative number flips big and small, so track the smallest run ending here as well as the largest.
keyTakeaway: Carry hi and lo, the largest and smallest products of a run ending at i. The next element x extends one of them or starts fresh: hi = max(x, hi · x, lo · x) and lo = min(x, hi · x, lo · x), both from the old values. The answer is the largest hi seen. One pass, O(1) space.
explanation:
This follows Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm) with sum changed to product. Given an integer array, return the largest product of a non-empty contiguous subarray. For [2, 3, -2, 4] the answer is 6, from [2, 3]. For [-2, 3, -4] it is 24, the whole array: two negatives make a positive.

Kadane's question still drives it: what is the best run that ENDS exactly at i? With sums, the best run ending at i was either nums[i] alone or the best run ending at i - 1 extended by nums[i]. With products that breaks: multiplying by a negative turns the largest product into the smallest and the smallest into the largest. In [-2, 3, -4], the best run ending at 3 is 3, but the one that wins at -4 is -6 (the smallest run ending at 3) times -4.

So carry two values: hi, the largest product of a run ending here, and lo, the smallest (the most negative). For the next element x the candidates are x alone, hi · x and lo · x; hi becomes the largest of the three and lo the smallest. Compute both from the OLD hi and lo, so save one before overwriting it. Start hi, lo and the answer at nums[0], as in the parent lesson, so an all negative single element still works. A zero resets both to 0, and the next element starts fresh because "x alone" is a candidate.

It is still one pass with a few variables: O(n) time, O(1) space. As with sums, the restart rule is what makes it work: a run is only worth extending if what came before helps, and with products "helps" can come from either extreme.

The visualization runs [2, 3, -2, 4, -1]; the message shows hi and lo after each element.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences comparing this with Kadane's algorithm for sums. Why is "the best run ending here" still the right subproblem, why does one value per index stop being enough, and what does a zero do to the runs?

visualizationSteps.message: Start at nums[0] = 2: hi = lo = best = 2. hi and lo are the largest and smallest products of a run ending here.
x = 3: candidates x = 3, hi · x = 6, lo · x = 6. So hi = 6, lo = 3.
x = -2: candidates x = -2, hi · x = -12, lo · x = -6. So hi = -2, lo = -12. x is negative, so the old smallest run gives the new largest.
x = 4: candidates x = 4, hi · x = -8, lo · x = -48. So hi = 4, lo = -48.
x = -1: candidates x = -1, hi · x = -4, lo · x = 48. So hi = 48, lo = -4. x is negative, so the old smallest run gives the new largest.
Done: the largest product is 48, from the whole array: the two negatives cancel. A sum based Kadane that kept only hi would have stopped at 6.

recognitionSignals: Best contiguous run under multiplication, or any operation where a negative can turn the worst value into the best.
Kadane's single pass feels right, but signs flip the comparison, so the minimum matters too.
gotchas: Compute the new hi and lo from the OLD values; updating hi first and then using it for lo is wrong.
Start from nums[0], not 1 or 0: [-2] must return -2.
Include x alone as a candidate, or a zero would wipe out every later run.
confusableWith: Greedy: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm) tracks one best run ending here; for products you need the largest and the smallest, because a negative swaps them.
Prefix sums answer subarray SUM questions by subtraction; products have no equally safe division because of zeros, which is why the one pass carries running extremes instead.

complexity.note: One pass with three variables: the largest and smallest products of a run ending here, and the best so far.

referenceSolutions.python:
def max_product(nums):
    hi = lo = best = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        a, b = hi * x, lo * x  # both from the OLD hi and lo
        hi = max(x, a, b)
        lo = min(x, a, b)
        best = max(best, hi)
    return best
